Issued at 320 AM CST Sat Nov 21 2026

THIS WEEKEND:

Warm, moist advection continues this morning, ahead of an 
approaching cold front, with 3AM temperatures in the 50s to lower 
60s. While coverage of showers has decreased over the last few 
hours, with only a few spotty showers remaining over the Arrowhead, 
starting to see radar returns fill in across central MN back into 
the Dakotas. Much of this is not hitting the ground yet, but as the 
cold front moves eastward, additional showers are expected to 
develop across the Northland this morning. Frontogenesis along the 
front will allow for a more organized line of showers, initially 
along the I-35 corridor this morning, then shifting eastward across 
northwest WI this afternoon through tonight. 

Rainfall and liquid-equivalent precipitation amounts remain fairly 
light, with most of the area receiving less than 0.10 inch of 
additional rainfall. Portions of the I-35 corridor northward along 
the North Shore could see around 0.25 inch through Sunday. With 
slightly better forcing and moisture over northwest Wisconsin, 
rainfall amounts around 0.25-0.50 inch are possible. There is a 40-
50% chance of more than 0.50 inch from I-35 and the North Shore 
eastward. By Sunday morning, the chances for more than 1 inch of 
rainfall increase to 40-50% east of Hayward to Ironwood.

Colder air wrapping around on the back side of the departing low-
pressure system tonight into Sunday will combine with cold-advection 
and additional shortwave troughing aloft to produce scattered, light 
showers. This shower activity should gradually transition from rain 
to a rain/snow mix to light snow throughout Sunday from northwest to 
southeast. This snow ends for most of the area by Sunday night, but 
light lake-effect snow is forecast to linger into Monday morning for 
the South Shore lake-effect snowbelts before drier air moves in. 
While not a locked-in scenario, the combination of steep low-level 
lapse rates, a small amount of MLCAPE (25-50 J/kg), and 20-25 mph 
northwest winds could produce snow squall potential (20-30% chance) 
Sunday afternoon into early evening for north-central Minnesota into 
the Arrowhead. Some hindering factors to travel impacts from these 
snow showers would be above freezing air and road temperatures, with 
highs in the mid-30s for much of the afternoon as well as lighter 
snowfall rates/accumulations. However, accumulations on roadways 
could have better potential to stick after sunset as air 
temperatures drop below freezing. Trends in snow squall potential 
will need to be watched closely.
As of now, the main impact would be brief, rapid reductions in 
visibility as any snow showers pass over a given location.

Snow accumulation with this system continues to look light and 
relegated mainly to the Iron Range into the Arrowhead and areas 
north, as well as parts of the South Shore lake-effect snowbelts. 
The probability for 1 inch or more of snow in those locations is 30-
60%, with locally higher probabilities of 60-80% in the higher 
terrain of Iron County. Probabilities of 2"+ amounts are 40-60% 
chance in the higher terrain of Iron County and little to no chances 
elsewhere.

As for temperatures for the weekend, expect above average high 
temperatures today for most of the area. Areas north of the Brainerd 
Lakes area are already behind the cold front this morning and temps 
should remain steady this morning or gradually fall through the day. 
Additional record warm temperatures could be set again today along 
with record warm lows this morning. See the Climate section below 
for details. Cooler, more seasonably normal air moves into the 
Northland on Sunday behind the cold front.

NEXT WORK WEEK:

Cooler, more normal temperatures for late November and a primarily 
drier pattern sets up for much of next work week as high pressure 
moves through the Upper Midwest and Great Lakes. Expect high 
temperatures in the upper 20s to mid 30s on Monday to moderate 
slightly to the 30s for mid to late week. Lows will largely be in 
the teens to 20s, with a 20-30% chance for upper-single digits in 
the typical cold spots Monday night. Some troughing aloft on the 
backside of the high pressure Tuesday night into Wednesday could 
still bring very light snow chances back to the Northland, but a 
lack of moisture likely keeps this feature dry. Precipitation 
chances remain at less than 20%. The mid- and upper-level patterns 
diverge late next week into next weekend, so confidence is low in 
precipitation potential during that timeframe.
